name: Coding practices
blurb: Debug to root cause, test first, verify before done, review well, keep changes small, and use git as a safety net.
searches: agent skill systematic debugging root cause new release
TDD test-driven development Claude Code skill
AI code review skill checklist PR review agent
refactoring simplification YAGNI coding agent guidelines skill
git worktree workflow Claude Code skill branch finishing

tests.prompt: Our checkout test fails about 1 in 5 runs on CI with 'expected 3 items, got 2'. I already added a sleep(500) and it still flakes. Fix it.
tests.good: Doesn't add more sleeps or guess; builds a loop that reproduces the flake (runs the test many times), reads the error, forms ranked falsifiable hypotheses (race, shared state, test pollution), instruments one variable at a time; replaces the sleep with waiting for the actual condition; fixes the root cause with a regression test; removes debug logs; reports which hypothesis was right with evidence from repeated green runs.

tests.prompt: Add a discount-code field to the checkout API: codes are case-insensitive, expire, and can be used once per customer. Use TDD.
tests.good: Clarifies or states assumptions (stacking, where codes are stored); agrees the seam (public checkout function/endpoint); vertical slices of one failing test then minimal code, each seen failing for the right reason; covers case-insensitivity, expiry with a controlled clock, once-per-customer (with a race/unique-constraint note); mocks only external boundaries; runs the full suite; no unrequested features.

tests.prompt: Review this PR before I merge: it adds a 'refunded' order status and a refund endpoint that updates the order and calls Stripe.
tests.good: Pins the diff range; checks against the stated requirements; flags enum completeness (every switch/filter/display on order status), check-then-write races and idempotency on the refund, authz on the endpoint, Stripe errors and partial failure (DB vs Stripe consistency), and tests that mock only Stripe; labels findings Critical/Important/Nit with file:line and a concrete fix; notes strengths; ends with a clear merge verdict and reasoning.

tests.prompt: Since last week's release the invoices page in our Next.js app takes 6 seconds to load, and one customer saw another company's invoice total. Find the root cause of both, fix them test-first, and get the branch ready for a PR.
tests.good: States a short plan first: debugging.md, tdd-and-testing.md and verification.md here; the slow page through backend-databases (query-performance.md: EXPLAIN ANALYZE, N+1, a missing index); the leak through security (secure-coding.md: every query scoped to the caller's org). Treats the leak as Critical and fixes it first; bisects the release range if the cause isn't obvious; writes a failing test for each bug (cross-tenant read, query count) before fixing; states each root cause with evidence; runs suite, lint, typecheck and build fresh; doesn't push or open the PR without a yes; checks the Done means of all three crafts.

tests.prompt: Sentry keeps alerting on PAYMENTS-WEB-4K2: 'TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading id)' in the checkout page, about 400 events since Friday's release. Find out what's really going on and fix it, and make sure Sentry knows it's fixed once we ship.
tests.good: Pulls the actual issue (stack trace, breadcrumbs, release, affected browsers or users, first seen) through the Sentry MCP, Sentry CLI or an exported link instead of guessing from the title, with a read-only token that is never pasted into files or commands; maps the minified frame to source via the release's source maps and ties first-seen to a commit range (git bisect or git log on that release); reproduces it with a failing test that feeds the undefined value from the real code path before touching the fix; fixes the root cause (not an optional-chaining band-aid that hides the error) and removes any debug logging; commits with the issue reference in the form `Fixes PAYMENTS-WEB-4K2` so Sentry resolves it on release, and checks regression-reopen behaviour; runs the suite, lint and typecheck fresh; does not push, open the PR or mark the issue resolved without the user's yes.

tools.name: Git
tools.why: Version control behind essentially every project; the Stack Overflow 2025 survey puts GitHub at 81% of collaboration-tool use and Git is the substrate of all commit, branch, worktree and bisect work in this craft.

tools.name: GitHub
tools.why: GitHub is the most used code collaboration tool (81% in the Stack Overflow 2025 survey); PRs, review threads and CI checks are where review, feedback and verification happen, and `gh` plus the official MCP server are how an agent drives them.

tools.name: GitHub Copilot code review
tools.why: Built-in AI PR reviewer for any team already paying for Copilot; AI-review round-ups (Greptile, macroscope, dupple 2026) list it among the six leaders but behind CodeRabbit on signal to noise.

tools.name: CodeRabbit
tools.why: Ranked the top AI code reviewer in most 2026 round-ups (Greptile, Dupple, macroscope, techsy) with the best signal to noise and every Git host supported; also ships a CLI for pre-commit review from Claude Code.

tools.name: ESLint
tools.why: The standard JavaScript and TypeScript linter and the usual lint gate in pre-commit, verification and CI; it has an official MCP server (`npx @eslint/mcp@latest`).

tools.name: Prettier
tools.why: The default opinionated formatter in JS/TS repos and the formatter in the Husky plus lint-staged recipe; the guide already uses it in one pre-commit command.

tools.name: Ruff
tools.why: The dominant Python linter and formatter (about 50k GitHub stars); Astral's uv is the most admired technology in the Stack Overflow 2025 survey, and Ruff is the lint/format half of that toolchain.

tools.name: TypeScript compiler
tools.why: `tsc --noEmit` is the typecheck gate in the guide's pre-commit and verification steps, and TypeScript is among the most used languages in JS projects per the Stack Overflow 2025 survey.

tools.name: Husky
tools.why: The standard git-hook manager for JS projects (35k GitHub stars, with lint-staged at 15k); Lefthook (9k) and the Python pre-commit framework are the alternatives.

tools.name: Sentry
tools.why: The most common production error tracker, the source of 'fix this production exception' tasks, with an official remote MCP server (mcp.sentry.dev), an OpenAI-curated skill and Anthropic's connector directory listing.

tools.name: Chrome DevTools
tools.why: The default debugger for front-end bugs, and the official `chrome-devtools-mcp` has about 53k GitHub stars and ships debugging skills for agents.

tools.name: pytest
tools.why: The standard Python test runner and the one the TDD loop names; Python is a top-used language in the Stack Overflow 2025 survey.

tools.name: Python debugger (pdb and debugpy)
tools.why: Interactive breakpoint debugging is the usual step after a failing test; pdb ships with Python, and agent skills now exist for pdb/debugpy, Node inspect and lldb.

tools.name: Semgrep
tools.why: Widely used pattern-based static analysis for custom code-quality and security rules; vendor ships an MCP server (687 stars) and a skill (security neighbour is `security`).

tools.name: Biome
tools.why: Rust formatter and linter that replaces ESLint plus Prettier in a growing share of new JS/TS repos (about 26k GitHub stars).

tools.name: Visual Studio Code
tools.why: The most used development environment by far: 75.9% of respondents in the Stack Overflow 2025 survey (IntelliJ IDEA next at 27.1%). Its debugger (breakpoints, launch.json, attach), rename/extract refactorings, source control view and GitHub PR extension are where most practitioners debug, refactor and review; market leader even though agents rarely drive it directly.

tools.name: GitLab
tools.why: Second code host after GitHub: 35.6% of Stack Overflow 2025 respondents use it (GitHub 81%). Merge requests, review threads and approvals are where review and feedback happen for those teams; `glab` is the official CLI and GitLab ships an official MCP server (beta, Premium/Ultimate) that reads MR diffs, comments and pipeline status. Its CI pipelines belong to cloud-devops (GitLab CI/CD) and its scanners to security; this entry is the MR review workflow.

tools.name: React Developer Tools
tools.why: The official React extension and the standard way to see which components re-rendered, how long they took and why; every React performance guide starts with its Profiler, and in 2026 it feeds React Performance Tracks in Chrome DevTools. The re-render half of `react-nextjs-performance.md` depends on it but the guide names it only as 'React Profiler' in one line.

tools.name: JetBrains IDEs (IntelliJ IDEA, PyCharm, WebStorm)
tools.why: IntelliJ IDEA is the fourth most used IDE in the Stack Overflow 2025 survey (27.1%) and the reference for safe automated refactoring (rename, extract, change signature) and graphical debugging in Java/Kotlin and, via PyCharm and WebStorm, Python and JS shops. Not an agent entry point, so minor.

tools.name: Graphite
tools.why: The main stacked-PR tool: Cursor described it as used by hundreds of thousands of engineers when it bought Graphite in December 2025, and 2026 code-review round-ups list it among the leaders. The `gt` CLI splits big changes into small dependent PRs (the guides' 'small atomic changes' at PR level) and Graphite ships its own MCP (GT MCP) and AI review.
